articles.title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
articles.summary: Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company's models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down. That's according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation […]
articles.full_text:
AI Anthropic Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development.

AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development. by Robert Hart Nov 7, 2026, 12:30 PM UTC Link Share Gift Photo: Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow.

Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes .

Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI.

And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down.

That’s according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development.

The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer.

The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement.

They also come at a pivotal time for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to pump the brakes on AI development .

But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing.

Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development.

Here are some of the biggest takeaways.

AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress.

Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time.

That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains.

METR wrote that employees using Anthropic’s most capable internal model on average self-reported being around 12 times as productive at their respective work as they would have been without AI assistance, around double what staff had reported just a few months earlier while using Mythos 5.

Image: METR For now, much of that acceleration appears to be coming from AI assisting human researchers, rather than AI working independently, though METR warned that “there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” Notably, the researchers said they found no clear signs of diminishing returns or observable bottlenecks that could prevent “even faster acceleration.” Three of Anthropic’s newest AI models remain under wraps Anthropic’s researchers are using more advanced AI models than the rest of us, with a lot of the acceleration and productivity gains described by METR attributable to unreleased internal models.

Over the past six months, Anthropic has finished training three models it has yet to release, according to METR.

The pace of development is swift, with the models — codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 — completing training in July, August-September, and September-October, respectively.

METR also identified an unreleased model dating back to 2022, called Unreleased 2022. “These are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames,” the researchers wrote.

Anthropic is keeping key information secret Anthropic gave METR access to a host of non-public information, including confidential research, model performance data, and employee interviews as part of the research process.

It had no obligation to do so and by METR’s own admission, the AI lab “shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations.” This is commendable, but it is worth noting that Anthropic did not grant researchers unrestricted access, nor the kind of “employee-like” access it has promised other METR safety researchers as part of a separate program announced last month.

It is an important distinction, given the reputational benefits companies can gain from independent assessments, even when they come with significant restrictions.

And there were significant restrictions.

Anthropic had the power to redact information from METR’s final report — and it used that power extensively. “We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic.

For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative,” METR wrote on X.

METR reiterated those concerns throughout the report, highlighting other limitations on its access. “Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied.” METR repeatedly stressed the impact Anthropic’s redaction decisions had on its ability to communicate its findings and for others to assess what’s going on at the company.

It noted that much of the redacted evidence could have “multiple plausible interpretations,” making it difficult for the public to assess its findings, understand the uncertainties surrounding them, and judge the evidence themselves. “As a consequence [of the redactions], the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here,” the report said.

In the report, METR said Anthropic justified the redactions on the grounds that releasing the information could benefit its rivals.

However, METR said “most of the redacted information was very high-level,” even though it said it was not in position to comment whether redactions were justified commercially or not. “We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged in a lengthy post on X responding to METR’s findings. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” he said, adding that doing so would make the risks METR is concerned about “worse.” McCandlish said that it’s a trade-off, but maintained Anthropic had made the “right call” in deciding to redact the information.

He said the company plans to publish its own report on the speed of AI progress “in the coming weeks,” as well as new steps it’s taking to strengthen safety.

Anthropic is accelerating the very technology it warns is dangerous and faster than many expected The publication of METR’s report has provoked a fierce backlash among AI safety researchers and commentators, largely centered on an apparent contradiction at the heart of Anthropic’s approach to AI: The company has been one of the most outspoken advocates for safety and responsible development, yet the report suggests it is helping accelerate the technology toward a threshold many consider dangerous, while seemingly failing to live up to its own commitments to transparency and accountability.

For some, the findings suggest that even many of the field’s most aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative.

They indicate that recursive self-improvement — AI systems that can autonomously develop increasingly powerful successor systems without human intervention, potentially accelerating development dramatically — may be closer than previously thought, raising concerns about whether existing safety measures can keep pace.

While METR’s report only covers Anthropic, OpenAI said in September that it is “making strong progress” toward building an AI researcher that can “further progress on deep learning and alignment” by March 2028.

The report provides evidence about just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told The Verge the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in AI 2027 , an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027.

He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development.

Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster.

Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told The Verge that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering.

On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development.

Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also compared the findings to AI 2027 ’s timeline.

Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers permitted to investigate OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.” Frustration is mounting over Anthropic’s approach to safety Beyond highlighting the speed of AI development, the report has also fueled a growing sense of frustration over Anthropic’s role in driving that progress.

The company has been one of the most vocal proponents of responsible AI development — and no stranger to calling for others to slow down — yet appears to be racing ahead itself.

This report only builds on already heightened tensions from its IPO prospectus and future plans released last month .

Anthropic’s decision to heavily redact the report, citing grounds that revealing more could help its rivals accelerate their own development, has fueled accusations of hypocrisy.

Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027 , accused Anthropic of “recklessly gambling with our lives,” adding that “it is pretty rich” of the company to cite others going faster as a reason to redact information when it does “not appear to be slowing down much at all.” Anthropic declined to answer The Verge ’s questions about the report and ensuing criticism, instead directing us to McCandlish’s post.

The redactions have also renewed calls for greater transparency and independent oversight of frontier AI labs, which grew to new heights earlier this year following a spate of incidents involving rogue AI agents .

Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, told The Verge that it was concerning that companies, not governments, were effectively calling the shots on automating AI research. “For democratic oversight to work, independent evaluators need the freedom to explain why they reached their conclusions, governments need to assess the evidence themselves, and the public has to trust this process,” Rosen said. “The report was not sufficiently transparent about the evidence.” Pressure is building for more transparency from AI labs Hobbhahn echoed Rosen’s concerns, saying that much of the reaction to the report stems from the apparent gap between Anthropic’s public safety stance and its actions.

He pointed to the company’s decision to cancel part of the assessment designed to evaluate how much compute it allocates to safety work versus improving capabilities.

METR said the company said “this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on.” For Hobbhahn, the episode underscores the need for independent safety researchers to be embedded more deeply within AI labs, with significant access to internal systems and evidence.

While his organization stands to benefit from such arrangements — Apollo is taking steps toward becoming an embedded evaluator at frontier labs — he is far from alone in calling for stronger oversight of AI development.

Others have called for more direct action.

In a direct response to the report, New York state Assemblyman Alex Bores, a key figure shaping the Democrats’ AI agenda, called on Congress to “ban RSI, this year if possible.” With the blue wave of Democrats — many of whom campaigned against AI companies — taking office soon, the prospect of tougher restrictions is a very real possibility.

And with AI research showing little sign of slowing down, the pressure is set to intensify.

Hobbhahn said he had another takeaway from the report, too: “Brace for craziness,” he said. “It is going to go very fast,” likely way too fast for society or politics to keep up.

articles.title: Claude can now analyze your spending with its new Personal Finance tool
articles.summary: With Personal Finance in Claude, users can connect their bank and card accounts through Plaid and ask questions about their finances.
articles.full_text:
Anthropic announced Thursday that Claude is getting a new tool called “Personal Finance,” designed to help users keep track of their money.

With it, users can connect their bank and credit card accounts through Plaid and ask Claude questions about their finances.

Anthropic says access is read-only, meaning Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest users’ money.

By letting Claude connect directly to bank and credit card accounts, Anthropic is positioning its chatbot as a financial companion that can help people understand their spending and make sense of their money, rather than simply offering them generic advice.

With the launch, Claude is playing catch-up to OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which introduced similar personal finance tools in May that also let users connect their financial accounts and ask questions about everything from spending patterns to long-term financial planning. “Claude gives you answers in everyday language, from your balances and transactions, and explains any term that’s new to you,” Anthropic wrote in a blog post. “Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer.” For instance, at the end of the month, a user could ask Claude, “Where did my money go this month?” The chatbot will then add up spending across the connected accounts and sort it by category, such as rent and utilities, food and drink, and shopping.

Users can choose to go deeper by following up with questions like, “Is that more than usual?” or “Anything else I’m missing?” Anthropic says the tool goes beyond basic spending summaries by analyzing transactions across connected accounts to flag potential issues, such as duplicate charges, unexpected fees, and steadily increasing bills.

Users can also ask broader questions about their finances, such as whether they’re spending more than they earn.

The tool can also explain financial concepts like APR (annual percentage rate), while providing calculations that show users how much they’ve paid in interest over the past year.

Of course, some people will have reservations about connecting their financial accounts to an AI chatbot.

Anthropic says Claude’s access is limited to each connected bank’s name, account name and type, the last four digits of the account number, balances, credit limits, and up to two years of transaction history.

Additionally, the company notes that when users chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren’t used to train its models.

Personal Finance starts rolling out in beta this week to users on the Pro, Max, and Ultra plans in the U.S.

The launch of the new tool comes as Anthropic has been expanding Claude into new verticals.

For instance, Anthropic launched Claude for Legal and Claude for Financial Services earlier this year.

articles.title: What happened to Transmeta, the last big dotcom IPO
articles.summary: Transmeta was the last big IPO of the dotcom era, launching Nov 7, 2000. Some analysts call its $273 million IPO the last successful tech IPO until the Google IPO in 2004. Transmeta didn’t completely fit in to the dotcom The post What happened to Transmeta, the last big dotcom IPO appeared first on The Silicon Underground .
articles.full_text:
Dave Farquhar Retro Computing November 6, 2026 November 6, 2026 3 Comments Transmeta was the last big IPO of the dotcom era , launching Nov 7, 2000.

Some analysts call its $273 million IPO the last successful tech IPO until the Google IPO in 2004 .

Transmeta didn’t completely fit in to the dotcom era, because they were a hardware company.

But they were still a technology company, and if their plans had gone well, they would have sold their product to dotcoms, but it didn’t work out that way for them.

In this blog post we explore what happened to Transmeta.

Was Transmeta truly the last of the dotcoms?

I’ve heard Transmeta called the last successful IPO of the dotcom era, or the last of the big dotcom IPOs.

But it’s an oversimplification to say there weren’t any successful technology IPOs between Transmeta and Google.

One very notable exception is Paypal, who ran an IPO in February 2002 that raised $70.2 million.

The Register even hailed Paypal as the return of the Internet IPO.

And it wasn’t just that dotcom IPOs grew scarce after November 2000.

On February 7, 2002, Forbes stated that only 34 IPOs in total launched between September 11, 2001 and February 6, 2002, compared to 87 in the same-year-earlier period, and 240 between September 11, 1999 and February 6, 2000.

That date is significant.

Any bad news can spook investors, and the 9/11 attack did, in fact, spook investors.

So where the dotcom-era ended is a fuzzy line, but it makes sense to draw the line at Transmeta.

Technology IPOs and particularly Internet IPOs became much more scarce after Transmeta, and the size of the IPOs shrunk too.

The distinction of Transmeta being a technology stock, rather than an Internet stock, also suggests investors were already cooling on Internet stocks by November 2000.

What was Transmeta?

Transmeta was a CPU company, co-founded by Bell Labs alumnus Dave Ditzel, who had worked on Bell Labs’ CRISP, an early RISC architecture.

But Transmeta may be better known for their most famous employee than for any of their products.

When Linus Torvalds completed his degree, there was a great deal of speculation where he would take his day job.

Transmeta was not the place most technologists expected him to land.

But it allowed him to continue his work on the Linux kernel while staying close to a key part of the hardware, the CPU.

In the year 2000, the CPU wars were cooling down.

A few years earlier, there had been four companies not named Intel producing Socket 7 CPUs.

But only two of them survived to compete in the next generation, and only AMD was able to compete at anything other than the entry level .

And even though the Cyrix name survived, it was the competing IDT technology under the hood.

How its CPUs worked Transmeta wanted to take a different approach.

They were going to produce an x86 compatible CPU, but they were going to use a translation layer to do it.

They would design a very efficient CPU, and in theory, they could place any translation layer in front of it that they wanted.

Emulating PowerPC or ARM would have been possible if they saw the need to do it.

But the popular yet inefficient x86 architecture was a more inviting target.

AMD was doing something similar, essentially translating x86 instructions into RISC instructions for efficiency, but they did it in hardware rather than software like Transmeta did.

AMD never had any designs on putting any different translation layer in front of it.

Transmeta did ship two CPUs, but weren’t able to reach the same levels of performance AMD and Intel were reaching.

Its first CPU, Crusoe , could run at Pentium III -like speeds but was about 30% less efficient, so a 700 MHz Crusoe ran like a 500 MHz Pentium III.

Transmeta didn’t have fabrication plants of its own, so IBM handled manufacturing of its first-generation CPUs.

The Transmeta Efficieon, released in 2004, competed with the Pentium 4 but peaked at 1.7 GHz.

With the Pentium 4 reaching 2.4 GHz speeds, the Efficieon had trouble competing.

And AMD’s release of the Athlon 64 didn’t help matters.

Selling 32-bit CPUs in a 64-bit world was going to be tough.

TSMC and Fujitsu handled manufacturing for the Efficieon.

Transmeta CPUs saw use in low-power laptops, thin clients, and embedded applications.

The Bluecoat web filtering appliance used them for a while.

But if you owned a computer at that time, it’s much more likely to have had an AMD or Intel CPU in it.

If you used one at work, it was even more likely to have an AMD or Intel CPU in it.

What happened to Transmeta Even though Transmeta was the last big dotcom era IPO, they were not among the survivors.

Torvalds resigned from Transmeta in June 2003.

What happened to Transmeta was that in 2005, Transmeta shifted to licensing intellectual property rather than selling CPUs.

And in January 2009, Transmeta sold itself to Novafora, who in turn sold the patent portfolio to Intellectual Ventures, a private equity company.

Novafora ceased operations in August 2009, just seven months later.

Intellectual Ventures licenses the Transmeta intellectual property to other companies on a non-exclusive basis.

Transmeta ended up being more like Netscape or VA Linux than Red Hat .

Today, Transmeta hardware is rare enough to be interesting as a collectible.

But there aren’t a lot of people nostalgic for it, and that probably keeps prices low.

articles.title: Airbnb says it’s launching an AI travel agent in the first half of 2027
articles.summary: Airbnb says its upcoming AI agent will help travelers plan trips, compare options, manage bookings, and get assistance throughout their stay.
articles.full_text:
Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027.

In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday , Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot.

In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot.

He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip.

Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month.

Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything. “Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment.

But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational.

Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.

In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips.

People want to look at photos.

They want to compare homes.

They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that.

So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said.

Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would. “What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy — which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components — maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries — and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.” The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs.

In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform.

The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself. “Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip — from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support.

These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote.

Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences.

Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year.

While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027.

The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates.

It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens. “Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing.

Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added.
